title: session-aware-tool-call-surface-design-prd
content:
Purpose:
This is a working PRD exploring a session-aware client contract for progressive streaming + tool-calling with typed frames and explicit fallback semantics. The goal is a pragmatic SDK surface that: reduces integration friction for tool-enabled apps, provides predictable low-latency flows, and provides observability for per-tool cost/latency while preserving compatibility with existing incremental streaming APIs.

Context and motivation:
- We have many hosted streaming PRDs; this takes a different tack: treat the client session as the first-class primitive. Sessions carry routing hints, model preferences, cached KV affinity, and a lightweight capability registry (which tools are available and their handshake info).
- Problem: apps that integrate tools often duplicate orchestration logic (tool selection, retries, fallback to simpler models, and streamed partial outputs). This leaks complexity into client code and increases end-to-end latency and error surface.

High-level proposal:
1) Session establishment phase (short-lived token handshake): client POST /v1/session -> returns session_id, capabilities, preferred_models, kv-cache-hash, stream_endpoint(s).
2) Streamed-interaction frames: each stream is a sequence of typed frames (meta, partial-text, suggestion, tool-invocation, tool-result, end). Frames are JSON objects streamed over server-sent events or WebSocket to support both browser clients and server SDKs.
3) Tool invocation frame semantics: tool-invocation contains: tool_id, input_schema, invocation_id, hints (sync|async|best-effort), cost_estimate. The runtime guarantees at-least-once delivery to the tool adapter and provides invocation lifecycle events (queued, started, result, error, fallback-engaged).
4) Fallbacks and graceful degradation: the server exposes a declarative fallback policy attached to the session: a prioritized list (primary model variant, cheaper quantized variant, remote fallback/hosted-tool-proxy). When a tool fails or latency crosses a soft threshold, the runtime can automatically fallback to a policy-specified alternative and emit a fallback frame to the client.

SDK ergonomics (surface sketch):
- JS/TS (browser + Node) should be the design driver. Offer a Promise-based openStream API that yields an async iterator of frames and a client.handleToolCallbacks(map) helper to register tool handlers.
- Example pseudo-code:

const session = await Redwood.session.create({ project: 'editor' })
const s = await session.openStream({ prompt: 'Summarize and call tools' })
for await (const frame of s) {
  switch(frame.type) {
    case 'partial-text': console.log(frame.chunk); break
    case 'tool-request':
      // user code may synchronously answer or let SDK forward to server-side adapters
      if (toolHandlers[frame.tool_id]) {
        toolHandlers[frame.tool_id](frame.payload).then(res => session.sendToolResponse(frame.invocation_id, res));
      } else {
        // opt-in: let server route to hosted adapter
      }
      break
  }
}

- Ergonomic principles: minimal ceremony to accept server-invoked tool requests; explicit opt-in for server auto-proxying of tool calls (security).

Structured output and typing:
- Support a typed-result frame carrying a JSON-schema id and the payload. SDKs should validate the schema client-side for early errors and provide a typed wrapper (TS generics) for comfortable integration.
- Provide a small schema registry (lightweight: URIs + optional version) returned during session creation. This lets model prompts reference structured output contracts without sending full schemas every call.

Observability and cost controls:
- Session-level telemetry: per-frame latency, per-tool invocation latency and token counts, fallback incidents, and total estimated cost.
- Expose cost-estimate frames before expensive tool invocations when cost_estimate > threshold configured by the customer. Client can abort or proceed.

Backward compatibility and migration path:
- Non-session legacy endpoints remain supported. Sessions default to server-assigned ephemeral session ids; session-based features are opt-in.
- Provide a compatibility shim in SDK that converts existing streaming text-only responses into frame streams (single partial-text frames). This allows clients to adopt session features incrementally.

Security and privacy:
- Tool-handshake must include a minimal attestation: tool owner, expected input schema hash, and required scopes. Clients must explicitly grant tokens for server-side tool proxying.
- Session tokens are short-lived (minutes) and auditable. Any tool-proxying action produces an audit event attached to the session id.

Edge cases and failure modes:
- Tool adapter silently returns non-JSON: emit tool-error frame and trigger fallback policy.
- Network partition during a stream: client can reattach using session_id + last_frame_id and request missing frames; server provides resumable offsets for partial-text and tool-invocation replay guardrails.
- Duplicate tool results on reattach: each invocation_id is idempotent at the adapter layer, and SDK applies a dedupe heuristic by invocation_id.

Open questions (needs engineering feedback):
- How much of the fallback policy should be editable by end users vs kept as platform controls?
- Do we require all tools to expose schemas or allow untyped tool payloads (and then tag them as opaque)?
- Should the session creation step support guaranteed affinity to a single runtime (for KV cache warmness) or rely on smart routing with sticky cache tokens?
- What is the right TTL for session tokens in mobile/browser contexts to balance UX and theft risk?

Acceptance criteria for MVP:
- Server-side: session create/openStream endpoints implemented; frame protocol over SSE or WS; hosted-tool proxy adapter skeleton with lifecycle events; fallback-engine basic ruleset.
- SDK: JS async-iterator stream abstraction; simple tool handler registration; typed-result validation using registry; reattach helper.
- Observability: per-session cost & latency metrics in Console (per-route breakdown) and events emitted for fallback triggers.

Rollout plan:
- Week 1–2: API prototype + adapter mock, SDK experimental package (alpha).
- Week 3–4: Internal dogfood (solutions team) with an example app (email composer + calendar tool flow).
- Week 5: Console telemetry integration + conservative feature flags in hosted API.
- Week 6: Early access customers and iterate on fallback policies.

Risks and mitigations:
- Complexity in SDK: keep minimal API surface (one stream, one registerHandler call). Move advanced features behind opt-in flags.
- Tool security exposure: opt-in server proxying and granular attestation tokens.
- Unexpected cost spikes from automatic fallbacks: require cost-estimate frames before auto-invoking expensive fallbacks for GA.

Action items (short):
- [ ] Eng: prototype frame format + SSE/WS handshake (owner: Miguel)
- [ ] SDK: prototype async-iterator and reattach helper (owner: Chen)
- [ ] Product: draft public-facing migration guide + customer opt-in checklist (owner: Aisha)
- [ ] Security: define tool attestation token shape and audit event schema (owner: Priya)

Notes to reviewers:
- This is intentionally permissive in early draft; looking for concrete feedback on: session TTL norms, schema registry ergonomics (embed vs uri), and fallback policy expressiveness.
- Please add inline comments or push to the linked PR prototype if you have code-level suggestions.
